articles.title: Trump fumed at coverage of rally cancellations before ordering the events back on
articles.summary: The decision to cancel relieved some political operatives on the ground, who were happy to hear Trump would be engaging in telerallies that tend to be more s...
articles.body:
Flying on Thursday to South Carolina to headline his 25th midterm rally this month, President Donald Trump and his political team made a decision, according to one of his advisers: Instead of holding an in-person rally this weekend in Kansas — a red state where Republicans appear vulnerable — Trump would deliver his closing argument there over the telephone.

A few hours later, another weekend rally in Iowa was similarly scrapped. It was a dramatic and sudden shift in the president's closing-stretch strategy, which had relied on boosting enthusiasm among his base through an exhausting blitz of conservative districts.

When Trump returned from South Carolina, he told reporters he didn't "feel I have to go to Kansas" because GOP Sen. Roger Marshall was "doing really well."

The decision relieved some political operatives on the ground, who were happy to hear Trump would be engaging in telerallies that tend to be more scripted.

"Thank God," one top Republican official told CNN, speaking on condition of anonymity to avoid alienating the White House. "He hasn't moved the needle anywhere."

Less than 24 hours later, the plans changed again. The rallies in Kansas and Iowa were back on, both now scheduled for Sunday. And the frenetic pace that White House officials had signaled was abruptly ending was now ramping back up.

Speaking at the White House on Friday afternoon, Trump said he'd received calls from friends in Iowa and Kansas asking him to reconsider the cancellations.

"We have a couple of races that are very important," he said. "And they said if you could go it would be better than a telerally. And I tried to talk him out of that and I said, 'What about a telerally?' But they asked me. So I'm going to do two on Sunday."

He also cited Saturday afternoon college football games as a reason for moving his events to Sunday.

Officials said the schedule had merely been rearranged to allow more time for Trump to dial into virtual events. But people familiar with the matter described different motivations to CNN.

After signing off on the changes, Trump had grown irked over the media coverage about his decision to cancel his final rallies, those people said. His irritation was apparent when he returned from South Carolina and lashed out at a reporter who questioned why he called off the events.

"You've been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect," Trump said when asked how he was feeling and whether he was sick of campaigning. The reporter who asked, Trump seethed, looked "like hell."

The president demanded the rallies be reinstated, the people familiar said, sending staff who had just worked to pull the events off the calendar scrambling to put them back on.

"Rallies are BACK ON!" read a statement confirming the change.

The episode only underscored how heavily Republicans' midterm prospects have relied on Trump's personal whims, from endorsements of his preferred candidates — some of whom are now struggling — to his signature rallies, which regularly veer away from the issues and talking points many candidates have tried to highlight.

Even some Republican candidates have scrambled to keep up.

"I think that I'm doing so well in the polls that he's got, probably got better places to spend his time," Marshall told reporters after news of the Kansas cancellation emerged Thursday.

Trump advisers insist the president remains a sought-after presence on the campaign trail, and his political team continues to field calls from GOP campaigns asking if he would visit their states in the sprint to Tuesday's elections, one adviser told CNN.

That was what Trump officials argued was the original rationale for canceling his events this weekend: by skipping in-person events, Trump could maximize his time conducting telerallies for candidates across multiple states. Multiple sources familiar with the planning did not contradict that rationale.

By Thursday evening, Trump's super PAC, MAGA Inc., had announced the president would headline virtual events in 19 states intended to "energize voters, drive turnout, and help deliver victories."

The switch to virtual events was not unwelcome in some Republican corners. In the 21-hour stretch of time that the in-person events were canceled, several GOP operatives in battleground states quietly expressed a sigh of relief that the Trump roadshow would no longer be coming to their states.

Many pointed out that Trump is less likely during telerallies to meander into the obscure topics that now consume major chunks of his rallies: the cognitive tests he claims to have aced, the White House ballroom, the bodies of various Republican men.

One Republican official said the Trump rallies were too time-consuming during a peak period when GOP activists would otherwise be door-knocking, canvassing and doing other get-out-the-vote activities.

Trump has pressed his aides at times to schedule more travel in the campaign's closing weeks, people who have spoken with him said, invigorated by the adoring crowds he's encountered in deep-red districts and encouraged by friends and advisers who have told him his presence is directly boosting Republican enthusiasm.

Yet at other moments during the monthlong barnstorming, those people said, he's bemoaned the breakneck nature of a tour that has taken him to a new town nearly every day — oftentimes to rally voters in college arenas or civic centers that appear downright miniature compared with the sold-out stadiums he played during his own campaigns. Trump has also griped privately, and increasingly in public, about how hard he's having to work down the stretch for a campaign that's not his own.

"I have to tell you a little secret," Trump said during an October 23 rally in a Florida arena that sat fewer than 5,000 people. "Outside, there's a crowd about two or three times this size, and I looked at my people with anger. I said, couldn't you have gotten us a larger arena than this?"

Later, as Trump boasted about the economy, he joked that he was "wasting my time" with the speeches and should just go home and let his accomplishments speak for themselves — a bit that he repeated at subsequent rallies.

The president has visited nearly every state on the Senate battleground map aside from Maine — many more than once. The initial White House decision to cancel the weekend Midwest appearances caused tremendous buzz, but few complaints among party stalwarts.

"Everyone has seen the president who wants to see him," the second GOP official said.

Trump will travel Friday to Daytona Beach, Florida, for a rally with Republican candidates for Senate and governor, and he is expected to spend part of the weekend at Mar-a-Lago, where an annual Halloween party is planned.

Including Sunday's events, Trump will have headlined 28 rallies since the start of October. Even he has acknowledged the schedule is a grind and that it has taken a toll on his voice.

"I don't need to do this. But I have to because if (Democrats) win the midterms, all of a sudden you're gonna see a slide and all of the crap that we talk about," he told a crowd in Kentucky this month. "That's why I'm here working my ass off for you."

This story has been updated with additional details.

articles.title: US appeals court again rejects Trump bid to set aside California ballots
articles.summary: The 9th Circuit Court calls the petition to remove 20,000 ballots from California’s vote count unconstitutional.
articles.body:
For the second time in less than a week, a United States appeals court has rejected a petition from the administration of President Donald Trump to set aside 20,000 ballots in California over concerns about non-citizen voting.

The decision came down on Friday, with less than four days until the November 3 midterm elections.

The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that Trump’s request would violate the US Constitution and risk disenfranchising eligible voters.

“The consequence of the United States’s request is not merely ballot segregation, but ultimately both the cancellation of the ballot and the removal of voters from the voting rolls,” the majority wrote in its ruling.

Judges Mark Bennett and Gabriel Sanchez – appointed by Trump and his Democratic predecessor Joe Biden, respectively – formed the majority.

A third judge, Trump appointee Patrick Bumatay, issued a dissent, saying the administration’s petition was a “reasonable request”.

The Trump administration has claimed that nearly 20,000 “likely non-citizens” received mail-in ballots to vote in California’s midterm elections on November 3. It sued the state on October 15 to prevent those ballots from being counted.

But the accuracy of the Trump administration’s list has been called into doubt, as have its claims of widespread non-citizen voting.

Election fraud in the US is extremely rare. So is non-citizen voting, despite Trump’s assertion earlier this year that as many as 278,000 foreign nationals across the country were registered to vote.

Like California, states such as Nevada and Washington have also received lists of alleged non-citizen voters, but officials there have found the documents largely inaccurate.

In Nevada, for instance, state authorities issued a statement in September saying the Trump administration had erroneously identified citizens as non-citizens on its list. Not a single name was correct, according to the statement.

California, a Democratic stronghold, will elect 52 members of the House of Representatives, one of Congress’s two chambers, on November 3.

The state has long been Trump’s target for criticism, with the president accusing its Democratic leadership of “cheating” in elections.

But California officials, including Governor Gavin Newsom, have countered that the Trump administration is seeking to meddle in the state’s elections to sow voter distrust and undermine the results.

“This is a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters,” Newsom said in a news release after the October 15 lawsuit.

Non-citizen voting in federal elections is against the law in all 50 US states, including California.

The Constitution’s Elections Clause also grants states exclusive authority to administer elections, though it does allow for Congress to pass regulations concerning voting procedures.

The Trump administration initially sent California its list of 20,000 “likely non-citizens” on October 12, barely three weeks before the midterm election.

California officials refused the administration’s demand to set aside the 20,000 ballots, requesting proof that the names on the list were indeed foreign nationals. According to the California government, no such evidence has been provided.

The Trump administration last week charged 28 foreign nationals in California with election-related infractions, but some of the accused told the Los Angeles Times they had never registered to vote.

The newspaper’s reporting suggested some of the non-citizen defendants shared the same name as eligible voters.

As the October 15 lawsuit navigated the court system earlier this month, the Trump administration sought an emergency ruling from the 9th Circuit Court to suspend the 20,000 ballots.

But the appeals court rejected the petition on Monday, saying the Trump administration had not given lower courts adequate time to weigh the matter.

A lower court ultimately ruled against the Trump administration on Wednesday, and the administration again appealed to the 9th Circuit Court.

In its majority decision, the appeals court framed the Trump administration’s lawsuit as an attempt to violate the Constitution’s Elections Clause.

“We decline the United States’s invitation to contravene the Elections Clause by undermining the Constitution’s plain text,” the majority wrote.

The majority also wrote that it had “major concerns” that granting the Trump administration’s request would “harm the public interest by risking the disenfranchisement of eligible voters and putting the entire tabulation process in jeopardy”.

articles.title: The final countdown: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, we have the latest midterm campaign trail updates from our reporters in the field. Plus, Kristen Welker shares the top Senate races she will be watching Tuesday. — Adam Wollner The final countdown With the midterm elections reaching their conclusion in just four days, NBC News reporters are spread out across the country, speaking with candidates, operatives and voters about the dynamics shaping the biggest races on the map. Here are our latest dispatches from the campaign trail. Ohio governor: The fallout from Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign ad featuring the estranged mother of his opponent, Amy Acton, has been a galvanizing moment for Democrats in a state that became redder with President Donald Trump’s rise in politics after a long run as one of the nation’s most competitive battlegrounds, Henry J. Gomez reports from Liberty Township. A private poll paid for by a Republican group this week showed Ramaswamy trailing Acton by 8 percentage points — a 6-point drop from an earlier survey, said a GOP strategist who works on Ohio races. Similar numbers have rattled around Republican circles for days. Michigan Senate: During a campaign event for Republican Mike Rogers, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, described Democrat Abdul El-Sayed — who, if elected, would be the first Muslim senator — as “a theocratic zealot” and “jihadist leprechaun” whose election would put American service members at risk because, if presented with national secrets, he would be likely to share them with terrorist groups. Cruz, like other Republicans, sought to link El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, a group the Democrat has condemned. As Allan Smith writes from Grosse Pointe Woods, Cruz’s message has become a staple of the anti-El-Sayed messaging, with Republicans leaning into the theme in advertising and at campaign events. And they’ve been echoed by some voters. Georgia governor: While the Southern battleground has two marquee contests on the ballot next week, only the race for the state’s top job between Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson remains tight. In the Senate race, polls broadly show Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff with a sizable lead over his Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins. Bottoms and Jackson both have their eye on winning over a potentially critical slice of the electorate that is supporting Ossoff in the Senate race in the final stretch of the race, Adam Edelman reports from Atlanta. Bottoms has campaigned alongside Ossoff and run ads touting his endorsement, while Jackson has backed away from casting himself as a staunch ally of Trump as he did during his GOP primary. New Hampshire Senate: Trump has spent nearly every day this month crisscrossing the country to turn out Republican voters in tight Senate races. But he’s steered clear of the Granite State, which he lost in all three presidential contests. Republican John E. Sununu is reminding the state’s fiercely independent voters that he is not tied to Trump, Brennan Leach and Julie Tsirkin note from Rye. He tells voters in a direct-to-camera TV ad released this month: “I’ve never even met the man!” Closing message: On the airwaves, Democratic Senate candidates have been far more likely to reference corruption, high costs and Trump, while Republicans have been more focused on immigration, crime and transgender issues. That’s according to an analysis from Bridget Bowman of more than 600 TV ads that launched in October. The key Senate races I’m watching on election night Analysis by Kristen Welker Can Democrats turn their recent momentum in red and purple states into a Senate majority? While the battlefield has expanded in recent weeks, here are the races I will be keeping a particularly close eye on next Tuesday. Michigan: The contest between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers will be a critical test of whether a progressive candidate can win in a swing state as Democrats start to fix their eyes on 2028. President Donald Trump won Michigan by less than 1 percentage point in 2024, but voters in a state driven by the auto industry are grappling with high gas prices and costly trade wars with neighboring Canada. Still, Michigan represents one of Republicans’ few pickup opportunities, and if they are able to flip it, that would give them a major boost as they try to maintain Senate control. Ohio: Sen. John Husted, who was appointed to the seat previously held by Vice President JD Vance, is facing off against former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat who is on a comeback tour after losing to GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno in 2024. The race has been affected by the governor’s contest, where Republican Vivek Ramaswamy ran that controversial ad featuring Democrat Amy Acton’s estranged mother. articles.title: Bessent alleges anti-fraud guardrails are ‘loosest’ in blue states
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Democratic-led states Friday of having poor fraud prevention mechanisms while at a Minnesota press conference. The state has been at the center of a healthcare fraud scandal for much of this year after the Justice Department indicted more than a dozen people on accusations of defrauding taxpayers, using funds for…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Democratic-led states Friday of having poor fraud prevention mechanisms while at a Minnesota press conference.

The state has been at the center of a healthcare fraud scandal for much of this year after the Justice Department indicted more than a dozen people on accusations of defrauding taxpayers, using funds for improper billing and childcare fraud, among other allegations.

And while Minnesota is not the only state the Trump administration targeted with fraud investigations, it has become a focal point of its anti-fraud agenda.

“In Minnesota, alongside other senior U.S. officials, U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent today announced several initiatives to combat the rampant fraud that has wasted billions of dollars in Minnesota,” a release from the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network said.

Bessent accused Democrats of letting fraud happen in states they govern, though he acknowledged such crimes also occur in red states.

“The Democrats [have] let this happen on their watch,” Bessent said. “It’s going on everywhere, and we’re going to track them down. But I can tell you that the guardrails tend to be loosest in the Democratic states.”

A congressional study published in 2023 found that Texas, a red state, had the most Medicaid fraud dollars in 2022 with $219.9 million, followed by California, Florida and Louisiana.

Bessent responded to a question about why they were singling out Minnesota, saying that per capita, the state has been one of the worst at fraud oversight. He placed the blame for this “lack of oversight” on Gov. Tim Walz (D) and his administration.

“The kind of egregious nature of this and the lack of oversight from the AG’s office and from the Walz administration is shocking,” Bessent said. “Minnesota, unfortunately, because of the lack of oversight, likely has as a percent of the dollars one of the largest in the country.”

A Walz spokesperson did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

The Trump administration has punished blue states over fraud accusations, freezing more than $1 billion in Medicaid funds for Minnesota and California this summer.

Earlier this year, Vice President Vance began chairing the White House’s anti-fraud task force, aiming to coordinate a national response to fraud at the local and state level. Trump said Vance would focus primarily on blue states in his role as “fraud czar.”

“His focus will be ‘EVERYWHERE,’ but primarily in those Blue States where CROOKED DEMOCRAT POLITICIANS, like those in California, Illinois, Minnesota (Somalia beware!), Maine, New York, and many others, have had a ‘free for all’ in the unprecedented theft of Taxpayer Money,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in April.

Last week, Trump announced a $25 million whistleblower program promising cash payments to those whose tips about fraudsters lead to convictions.

articles.summary: A deceased Goochland County beagle named Biscuit reportedly received a Virginia rights restoration certificate, prompting calls for an audit.
articles.body: A Southside Virginia lawmaker is demanding an investigation after a constituent received an official rights-restoration certificate for his dog, Biscuit, a beagle-hound mix from Goochland County that died about five years ago. The discovery follows the "Betty No Last Name" controversy in Chesapeake — where a purported convict lacking a surname had "her" rights restored — and raises fresh questions about the governor's vetting process just days before voters decide whether to make felons' voting-rights restoration automatic via an Election Day ballot measure supported by Richmond Democrats. Del. Tom Garrett, R-Buckingham — who received the letter from the constituent who owned the pet — is now calling for an investigation into how Gov. Abigail Spanberger could have restored voting and jury-service rights to a deceased animal. DEM AG'S ELECTION CRUSADE AGAINST TRUMP RUNS INTO EMBARRASSING DEAD-FELON BLUNDER BACK HOME "This is not a question of whether people who have served their sentences deserve a second chance. This is a question of whether the Commonwealth is exercising one of the Governor’s constitutional powers with even the most basic level of review," Garrett said. "Biscuit was a dog. Biscuit has been dead for five years. Yet an official document bearing the governor’s signature says the executive reviewed the particulars of Biscuit’s criminal case and determined her rights should be restored. Virginians deserve an explanation for how that is possible." HIDDEN CALIFORNIA DESERT PET CEMETERY HOLDS UNEXPECTED PIECE OF WHITE HOUSE HISTORY Biscuit’s owner, who declined to be identified to avoid political backlash, confirmed the letter's authenticity to Fox News Digital and told Garrett in a statement that the pup was a "good dog and is greatly missed." "To my knowledge, she was never convicted of a felony, nor did she ever show any interest in voting," the owner said. Fox News Digital reached out to Spanberger for comment. A spokesperson for Spanberger replied, "Of course we did not restore the rights of a dog. We cannot disclose this individual's information, but we can tell you that it is associated with a person with a date of birth and Social Security number." Fox News Digital followed up to seek clarification on what error may have occurred but did not receive a response. The owner told Fox News Digital that Biscuit was never sent to the pound or had any other contact with Richmond that could have resulted in her being placed on the voting rolls. The owner said a sibling is currently incarcerated but added that the connection is moot because Spanberger’s stated effort only involves released former convicts. ELECTION DAY 2026: JOIN AMERICA'S CONVERSATION HERE! Garrett noted in a statement that the Spanberger administration said in July that Secretary of the Commonwealth Candi Mundon-King would be "proactively identifying Virginians who had lost their rights, confirming that those individuals were eligible, and restoring their rights," in his words. Spanberger announced in August that the initial figure of 66,000 had reached 100,000 individuals who had received restoration of their rights since the Democrat took office in January. TREASURY HAILS SUCCESS OF ANTI-FRAUD PROCESS THAT FLAGGED AND PREVENTED $99 MILLION IN PAYMENTS TO DEAD PEOPLE "The administration told Virginians these individuals were being identified and their eligibility confirmed," Garrett said in a statement, going on to call for an investigation into how a restoration certificate bearing Biscuit's name came to be issued. "The document itself represents that the executive reviewed the particulars of each case. If a deceased family pet made it through that process as a convicted felon, then we need to know what was actually reviewed, what databases were used, what safeguards existed, and how many other erroneous restorations were issued." An attorney in Fluvanna County when not legislating, Garrett said the Commonwealth must launch an immediate independent audit of Spanberger’s restoration-of-rights actions and disclose the underlying record that led to "Biscuit Rigsby" being identified as a convicted felon, as well as what Spanberger’s office defines as the "review of the particulars" of Biscuit’s case. Any investigation should also identify how many certificates and citations were issued to deceased, nonexistent or duplicate humans and require the immediate preservation of relevant data. WATCHDOG, GOP LAWMAKER WARN NY VOTER REGISTRATION SYSTEMS LACKS KEY SAFEGUARDS He said in a statement that his questions are not partisan and that Virginians who support restoring released felons’ voting rights should be outraged by Biscuit’s case. "At what point does rank incompetence and malfeasance become criminal conduct?" Garrett added in a video posted to social media. articles.title: Judge asks if Trump’s desire to rush triumphal arch in DC is to ‘bedazzle the city’
articles.summary: A federal judge on Friday was skeptical of the Trump administration’s urgency to rush construction of a controversial 250-foot triumphal arch that the presid...
articles.body:
A federal judge on Friday was skeptical of the Trump administration's urgency to rush construction of a controversial 250-foot triumphal arch that the president wants to begin next week.

Judge Tanya Chutkan asked an administration attorney, "What's the harm to the government to wait 3 or 4 months? What's the rush to put this arch up?," asking if the president's main desire is to "bedazzle the city."

Originally proposed as a monument for the country's 250th birthday, the Trump administration now argues the arch located in a traffic circle would serve both a tourist attraction and a military complex to store drones and ammunition.

Chutkan noted that while Trump has been espousing these military justification claims on social media for months, in their lawsuits the "government had appeared to back away from that position." The Obama nominee implied the Justice Department was "coincidentally" including national security interests in their argument now after the Supreme Court ruled in favor of the White House ballroom in August on similar grounds.

"We're not talking about plans for a cafeteria, how exactly does the administration plan to use this for national security?" Chutkan pressed the Justice Department attorney Robert Stander.

In response, Stander referenced repeated attempts on Trump's life, to which Chutkan countered, "The arch is somehow supposed to deter assassination attempts on the president? It's going to be completed 3years from now."

She also raised concerns with installing military equipment in an area the DOJ says will attract up to 22,000 civilian tourists a day.

The Justice Department argued that the challengers lacked standing, since the plans will not be finalized until next week's National Capitol Planning Commission meeting. However, the administration previously said that construction could begin that same day upon approval. Chutkan pointed out that following this logic, plaintiffs would only have one day to bring forward a lawsuit.

"What would be final agency action," she asked, "when bulldozers start digging up the ground?"

The group of veterans suing the administration requested an emergency court order to immediately halt construction of the arch, arguing it would undermine the sanctity of burial sites at Arlington National Cemetery. The proposed arch would obstruct the clear sightline of the row of national landmarks from the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery. Several of the veterans spoke in court Friday.

Chutkan told the plaintiffs she was not interested in any "distaste and disgust against the administration" but instead in how their personal experiences would be impacted by the looming arch.

She also appeared favorable to the argument that the veterans had more to lose than the plaintiff in the ballroom case who had cited aesthetic concerns, since they are active participants at Arlington National Cemetery, and the arch construction has not yet begun.

"The area is still pristine, the view is unobstructed, so why isn't this case more like the golf course case?" Chutkan asked.

Trump's arch faces another lawsuit from a county board in Virginia, so any future ruling from Chutkan will not be the end of the project's legal challenges.

articles.body:
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is warning that Republicans could lose as many as eight Senate seats in the midterm elections and get swept in all of the statewide Texas races, including the Senate contest between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico, if the GOP has a bad day on Nov. 3.

“The election is just a few days away, and all across the country there are Senate races that are incredibly close. There are eight to 10 Senate races across the country that are basically tied,” Cruz said on a Friday episode of his podcast, “The Verdict with Ted Cruz.”

“If we have a good night on Election Day, we could have a fantastic result. We could end up with 53 Republicans in the Senate. We could end up growing our majority in the Senate,” he said.

But he warned “if we have a bad day” Republicans “could wake up the day after Election Day, instead of 53 Republicans, with 45.”

“That big a delta is at play,” Cruz said after traveling to Georgia, Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina, Michigan and Iowa to campaign for GOP candidates.

Cruz said there will be “massive Democratic turnout” in the midterm elections and warned that Republicans face a potential “bloodbath” if Republicans don’t turn out to the polls in big numbers.

“I’m worried,” he said. “What we’re seeing across the country is massive Democrat turnout.

“Democrats are showing up, they’re energized, they hate, hate, hate Donald Trump,” he said. “If the election were over today, if just the early votes that have been cast so far are counted, Republicans would lose massively.”

But Cruz argued “there are Republican votes out there to turn that around” if GOP-leaning voters get motivated to vote.

He said reliable Democratic voters are showing up “in massive numbers.” But he said the reliable Republican voters aren’t voting early at the same rate as stalwart Democrats.

“Please, please, please show up and vote,” Cruz pleaded to his listeners.

He said there are more reliable Republican voters in the GOP-leaning Senate battleground states, but they need to cast their ballots to make a difference.

Cruz warned that the statewide races in Texas are extremely close and warned that Republicans could get swept in the Lone Star State if things go wrong for their party.

“Texas is excruciatingly close. Understand we could lose Texas,” he warned. “Not just the Senate race. We could lose every single statewide race in Texas. That’s how close these numbers are.”

He countered Republicans who argue the polls are wrong by saying while pollsters may show left-leaning bias on occasion, the data showing huge Democratic turnout this year is very real.

“I can tell you having run a lot of campaigns, having examined a lot of numbers, these data are not fake. The Democrats are massively out-turning out the Republicans. We got to fix that.”

Cruz’s Senate office did not return a request for comment.

articles.title: Justice Department requests separating Alaska ballots that rank Dan J. Sullivan in Senate race
articles.summary: The court filing, which cites the potential for “voter confusion,” did not spell out how segregating ballots would determine if a voter was confused.
articles.body: The Trump administration asked a federal judge Friday to issue an order before Monday directing Alaska election officials to segregate all ballots ranking Senate candidate Dan J. Sullivan as it continues its investigation into his candidacy. Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward wrote in a court filing that state officials should “preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary.” “These modest precautionary measures will be impossible after Election Day, so there is good cause for expedited consideration,” he added. The filing did not spell out a process for ballot review or explain how reviewing a ballot would show if a voter was confused about ranking the candidates. Alaska uses ranked choice voting, and there are four Senate candidates on the ballot. The Trump administration has ramped up its efforts to inject itself into the Alaska election, which by statute is handled by state officials, after The New York Times reported this week that Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan, a former school teacher, to run against Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. Peltola has denied any involvement in Sullivan’s campaign. Woodward, alongside Alaska’s top federal prosecutor, U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman, made three other filings Friday regarding the civil case the administration is pursuing in hopes of blocking Alaska from certifying the Senate election results. In one filing, the prosecutors requested expedited sharing of “internal and external conversations” from Peltola’s campaign “regarding its efforts to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan to run for office.” Another filing asks for the “Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee’s internal and external conversations regarding its efforts recruit Daniel J. Sullivan to run for office.” The DSCC has said it was “not involved with Dan J. Sullivan.” An additional filing seeks a preliminary injunction in the case. Friday’s filings came shortly after Heyman held a press conference in Alaska, where he acknowledged a parallel criminal case. Asked what potential crimes prosecutors are looking into, Heyman declined to provide details. “Because this is an ongoing investigative matter, we can’t discuss the specifics of those investigative steps, and who or may or may not be involved,” he said. “This protects the integrity of the investigation and it protects those who may be the subject or target of those investigations.” Heyman cited the recent reporting from The New York Times, saying the “new information has resulted in a significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska.” The Justice Department issued at least three dozen new subpoenas and document preservation requests as of Thursday, including subpoenas sent to the campaign offices of Peltola and of Dan J. Sullivan. President Donald Trump, who has urged legal action against Peltola and the second Sullivan, said Friday morning that he doesn’t know whether Sen. Dan S. Sullivan can win with the current ballot. “I will tell you, he’s a great senator, and what they tried to do, and he would, you know, he would have won,” Trump said in an interview with Kansas City talk radio host Pete Mundo. “I don’t know how he can win here because you’re splitting up the vote illegally. I think it’s a total fraud.” Trump has said repeatedly that Dan J. Sullivan should be removed from the ballot. In an interview with Fox News’ Sean Hannity earlier this week, Sen. Sullivan told supporters in Alaska how to mark up their ballot to best help him on Election Day. “So rank me first, Sullivan, Dan S. Registered Republican incumbent. That’s what the ballot says,” he said. “Rank the other Republican second, [Gerald] Heikes. Rank, I hate to say it, Sean, but in our screwed-up system, you rank the fake guy third, and then of course blank. Do not rank Peltola. Now that is the screwed up system we have.”

articles.body:
FDA unveils proposals to update infant formula nutrient requirements

The Food and Drug Administration is proposing to update nutrient requirements for infant formula, the first nutrition review for formula in nearly 30 years.

The review is part of the Trump administration’s Operation Stork Speed initiative, which was announced in March 2025 as part of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again movement.

“Parents deserve confidence in every bottle they feed their baby” Kennedy said in a statement. “We will hold infant formula manufacturers to rigorous scientific standards and put babies’ health first.”

The proposed rule — which is the first phase of the formula review — would update requirements for vitamin A, vitamin D, iodine and manganese as well as reaffirm existing requirements for chloride, potassium, selenium and sodium.

The review is being conducted in three phases , acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantis said, with the goal of releasing one final rule that will cover all 30 nutrients currently required, as well as potentially additional nutrients.

Personal injury and product liability attorney Bill Marler welcomed the update as long overdue and applauded the additional transparency, but noted the absence of a crucial issue that recently plagued the infant formula supply.

Nothing in the announcement “touches the hazard that actually put American babies in intensive care this year and last,” Marler wrote in a blog post.

“The words Clostridium botulinum do not appear in it. Neither do Cronobacter, Salmonella, nor the word pathogen. “

Since November 2025, 52 infants have been hospitalized with botulism after being fed powdered infant formula.

“Not one of them was hurt by a heavy metal or an outdated vitamin D requirement,” Marler said.

articles.title: Time to set back the clocks, much to Trump’s chagrin
articles.summary: Tick tock – clocks in America will fall back this Sunday. It could be the last time, if President Trump and some like-minded lawmakers get their way. But the debate over making daylight saving time permanent has proven divisive even within the president’s party. The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act earlier this year, which…
articles.body:
Tick tock – clocks in America will fall back this Sunday. It could be the last time, if President Trump and some like-minded lawmakers get their way. But the debate over making daylight saving time permanent has proven divisive even within the president’s party.

The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act earlier this year, which would end the semiannual clock change, but the Senate has yet to pick it up.

Trump has been a big proponent for the permanent change, slamming the Senate for “letting the Daylight Saving Bill die, when a vast Majority of the Country want it.”

“Most people are demanding light in the evening, but ALL want not to change their clocks anymore,” he wrote on Truth Social earlier this week. “TAKE A VOTE!”

Congress isn’t currently in session, and won’t be back until after the clocks change.

At his Mississippi rally on Monday, Trump called the clock change “ridiculous” and said it “drives everyone crazy, which nobody wants to do anymore.”

He pointed to data showing less crime is committed when there’s more light in the evening. Earlier this month, he argued the setback “costs our Country a fortune, is bad for Crime, stress on people, Sports, and just about everything else you can imagine.”

But voices on both sides of the debate can cite data proving their case.

Rep. Mary Gary Scanlon (D-PA) and Rep. Pat Harrigan (R-NC) introduced bipartisan legislation in July called the Sunshine for Our Kids Act that would establish a permanent standard time (the current norm from November to March).

They worry more sunlight in the evenings leaves mornings dark for schoolchildren and commuters.

“For decades, scientists and medical professionals have highlighted the detrimental mental and physical health impacts of twice-a-year clock changes, particularly on children and teens,” Scanlon said in a statement .

At least one Republican agrees with them: Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.), typically a staunch Trump supporter.

“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” he wrote in a post on X earlier this month. “Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first.”

An AP-NORC poll from last October found that 12 percent of U.S. adults favor the twice-a-year change, while 47 percent oppose it and 40 percent are indifferent about it.

Some 56 percent said they would prefer daylight saving time year-round, while 42 percent said they would rather standard daylight time year-round.

The golfing industry is a leading proponent of the argument that more daylight in the evenings is better for business – and the economy generally, with more people staying out after work and school.

“Overall, permanent DST is viewed as more beneficial to the golf industry, particularly for small business revenue, accessibility to the game, and general recreational enjoyment and benefits,” National Golf Course Owners Association CEO Jay Karen testified before a Senate committee last year.

“Our industry is uniquely tied to daylight, and the number of playable hours directly affects the number of rounds we can offer, the staff we employ, and the revenue we generate, especially in the late afternoon and early evening.”

An analysis from JP Morgan Chase Institute found that in Los Angeles, when compared to a city like Phoenix that does not observe daylight saving, debit card spending per capita rose at the beginning of daylight saving by 0.9 percent. However, spending dropped 3.5 percent following the end of daylight saving time.

Andy Owen, the director of advocacy communications at the National Association of Convenience Stores, said the association doesn’t take an official position on permanent daylight saving time “although we would be comfortable with it.”

“Shifting daylight to the end of the day tends to be good for business because it provides more time for shopping after regular work hours,” he said. “We want what’s good for businesses.”

Studies do support Trump’s argument that crime and accidents occur less with permanent daylight saving time. One study found that full-year daylight saving would reduce pedestrian fatalities by 13 percent and motor vehicle occupant fatalities by 3 percent.

Similarly, research has found that robberies drop about 7 percent for the entire day and 27 percent during the evening hour when sunlight is gained.

David Bieri, an associate professor at Virginia Tech, put together a brief on which states would benefit the most and least if daylight saving time was made permanent.

He found that permanent daylight saving time would pay off more in the north and on the eastern side of the time zones, like Seattle, Boston and Chicago.

“Permanent daylight time’s safety case is strongest in places like Boston and weakest in places like Indianapolis,” he said.

And while Trump said the twice-a-year clock change is “stress on people,” health associations like the American Academy of Sleep Medicine , the American Medical Association and the Society for Research on Biological Rhythms all say standard daylight time is better for health than daylight saving time.

“There’s the immediate hit and then there’s the slow burn,” Dr. Carla Finkielston, a professor with Virginia Tech’s Fralin Biomedical Research Institute, said of the health effects linked to the time changes.

“In the first few days after the spring change, researchers have reported shorter sleep, worse performance, a bump in heart attacks compared with neighboring weeks, and possibly more traffic accidents,” she said.

“The slow burn is the mismatch that sticks around, which we call social jetlag. Populations carrying more of that mismatch show higher rates of diabetes, obesity, heart disease, depression, and some cancers, along with shorter sleep and more trouble with mood and thinking.”

“The logic is simple enough. Standard Time is the arrangement where the clock on the wall sits closest to the sun overhead, so it asks the least of our biology,” she added.

While Trump has said the changing of the clocks is “a big inconvenience, and for our government, a VERY COSTLY EVENT,” studies have found that DST actually costs more.

Research from Chmura Economics & Analytics found that the total economic cost of DST in the U.S. is estimated at roughly $672.02 million annually, between lost productivity, injuries and accidents due to the sleep loss.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) doesn’t seem anxious to move on Trump’s daylight savings demands. He said earlier this month that there was no clear path for a successful vote on permanent daylight saving time in the Senate, despite the House passing the bill in a 308-117 vote.

Whether a Democratic majority would be inclined to make a change remains to be seen.

“The clock is shared infrastructure — a public good like weights and measures,” Bieri said. “When the evidence is a coin toss, Washington shouldn’t pick the option that once again favours the places that already have the most.”

articles.title: Feds ‘intensely’ probing alleged Alaska ballot scheme, US attorney confirms
articles.summary: Federal authorities are investigating whether Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign’s reported effort to recruit a candidate in the Alaska Senate race with the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) violated the law, the state’s top federal prosecutor announced Friday. U.S. Attorney for the District of Alaska Michael Heyman said during a press conference that…
articles.body:
Federal authorities are investigating whether Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign’s reported effort to recruit a candidate in the Alaska Senate race with the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) violated the law, the state’s top federal prosecutor announced Friday.

U.S. Attorney for the District of Alaska Michael Heyman said during a press conference that the investigation has been in the works for several months but that federal authorities are looking into the matter “intensely and swiftly” after “troubling new revelations” were reported by The New York Times this week.

The outlet reported Wednesday that Democratic operatives and Peltola’s campaign were involved in an effort to recruit a second Dan Sullivan to run in the state’s Senate race.

“This new information has resulted in a significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska, and I have assigned several attorneys in my office to assist in the matter as well,” Heyman said.

While the U.S. attorney would not disclose which potential crimes his office was looking into or whom it was targeting in the investigation, he emphasized a commitment to election security.

“What I can tell Alaskans is that we will not let anyone or any group undermine this election,” Heyman said.

Peltola, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and the incumbent senator’s GOP challenger , Dan J. Sullivan, have all denied any involvement in the reported effort to recruit spoiler candidates for the race.

“I just want to clear the air: I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent,” Peltola said during a Thursday evening speech in Juneau, Alaska. “That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters.”

This week, President Trump called for both Peltola and the spoiler candidate to be removed from the ballot and prosecuted . Additionally, Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) on Wednesday ordered an investigation into Peltola over the Times’s reporting.

“Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support,” the Republican governor wrote on social media . “Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections.”

On Friday, Heyman urged anyone with knowledge about the “Dan Sullivan issue” or other potential election integrity violations to contact federal authorities.

“Within the last 24 hours or so, we have received a number of new pieces of information that we’re following up on,” he said. “Anybody with additional information should contact the FBI as soon as possible.”

articles.body:
In Iowa elections, cancer crisis looms large

Rising cancer rates and a potential link to farm pollution are causing a crisis in Iowa, throwing uncertainty into the midterm elections in the state that has shifted ruby red in recent years.

© Abel Uribe, Chicago Tribune, Tribune News Service via Getty Images file

Iowa suffers from the second-highest rate of new cancer cases in the U.S. and it’s one of the few states where the number of cancer cases are rising. Across the state, the cancer crisis has become a major campaign topic ahead of the midterm elections.

Candidates from both parties have made tackling the environmental causes of cancer—and blaming “Big Ag”— a key part of their platforms. It’s an attack that would have been unheard of from Republicans in the Corn Belt hub.

The state has a series of blockbuster races this year including the governor’s contest between Zach Lahn (R) and Rob Sand (D), the Senate race between Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) and state Rep. Josh Turek (D) as well as several competitive House seats.

Lahn, in an unusual move for a Republican, is embracing not only the cancer issue, but also vowing to clean the water and regulate chemicals if he’s elected.

These issues aren’t falling neatly along party lines and some Democrats are making the case that they’re best-suited to tackle the problem.

“This cancer issue is resonating with people and almost everyone has a story here of a family member or someone else that has met an early demise,” Democratic agriculture secretary candidate Chris Jones, who is emphasizing water quality in his campaign, told The Hill earlier this year.

Welcome to The Hill’s Energy & Environment newsletter, I’m Rachel Frazin — keeping you up to speed on the policies impacting everything from oil and gas to new supply chains.

articles.title: RNC chair predicts GOP wins in Alaska, Texas, 3 other battlegrounds
articles.summary: Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Joe Gruters remained optimistic Friday evening about his party’s chances in next week’s midterms, predicting big wins in key battleground states despite troubling polling numbers for the GOP. Gruters told NewsNation’s Blake Burman he expects Republicans will win Senate races in Maine, Texas, Ohio and Alaska — all of which…
articles.body:
Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Joe Gruters remained optimistic Friday evening about his party’s chances in next week’s midterms, predicting big wins in key battleground states despite troubling polling numbers for the GOP.

Gruters told NewsNation’s Blake Burman he expects Republicans will win Senate races in Maine , Texas , Ohio and Alaska — all of which The Hill’s nonpartisan election forecasting partner, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), lean “narrowly” toward Democrats. He also predicted a GOP victory in North Carolina , which the handicapper says will “likely” go blue.

Burman pressed the RNC chair on generic ballot polling that displayed a disadvantage for Republicans running this election cycle. An Emerson College Polling survey released Friday found Democrats held a 10-point lead over Republicans on a generic ballot.

“We put up candidates that can win and common-sense mainstream candidates, and I think that will make the difference,” Gruters told Burman. “So yes, maybe the generic ballot, we’re not doing so hot, but when it comes to candidates that are well known and they’re getting their message out, yes, we do have the benefit.”

DDHQ places the Democrats’ chances of regaining control of the House this November at 82 percent, according to a Friday forecast . The party has a slimmer chance at retaking the upper chamber of Congress, with the nonpartisan election handicapper placing this probability at around 62 percent.

The RNC chair also addressed President Trump’s reversal on his decision to cancel two rallies set for this weekend in Iowa and Kansas. The president announced Friday the events were back on and will both be held in person on Sunday.

“Listen, all these decisions are being made in real time,” Gruters said. “I mean, we’re looking at data, looking at where we may need to help certain candidates and people, and so there may be some more changes.”

Gruters also weighed in on Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s (R) response to reports that Democratic nominee Mary Peltola’s campaign was involved in an effort to recruit a candidate in the state’s Senate race with the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R).

When asked by Burman whether the RNC would seek to stall the certification of this election if Peltola was successful, Gruters said he would “follow the governor’s lead.”

“We’ll see [where] that investigation ends up, but we’re going to be ready to help any way we can,” he said.

On Friday, the top federal prosecutor in Alaska announced his office was involved in a separate investigation into whether any laws were broken in this alleged spoiler candidate effort. Peltola and her campaign have denied any involvement in the candidate’s recruitment.

articles.title: MAPA: Como votaram municípios com maior presença evangélica no Brasil | G1
articles.standfirst: Cruzamento entre dados do Censo 2022 e o resultado do 2º turno das eleições presidenciais mostra que a religião acompanha o voto no Centro-Oeste e Nordeste, mas não no Sul nem no Norte do país. Veja como ficou a votação em Lula e em Flávio Bolsonaro.
articles.summary: Dados do Censo 2022 revelam que Flávio Bolsonaro venceu na maioria das cidades com mais de 30% de evangélicos, com forte adesão no Centro-Oeste e no Norte.
articles.body:
Presidente reeleito Lula e o candidato derrotado Flávio Bolsonaro — Foto: Paulo Pinto e Joédson Alves/Agencia Brasil

Derrotado por Lula (PT) no segundo turno das eleições presidenciais, o senador Flávio Bolsonaro ( PL ) teve seu melhor desempenho nos municípios onde os evangélicos pesam mais na população. É o que mostra o cruzamento entre os dados de religião do Censo 2022, do IBGE , e a votação de domingo (25), município a município. A totalização do TSE confirmou a reeleição de Lula para um quarto mandato, com 51,8% dos votos válidos, contra 48,2% do candidato do PL .

Nas cidades, o desempenho do senador variou de 7,6% a 90,5% dos votos válidos. Já a fatia de evangélicos na população ia de 1,2% a 88,7%. Para comparar as duas medidas, cada uma foi dividida em três faixas — baixa, média e alta —, o que resulta em nove combinações possíveis no mapa abaixo.

O retrato dessa associação está no Centro-Oeste. Ali, 42% dos municípios estão no grupo de maior presença evangélica e, ao mesmo tempo, de maior votação no candidato do PL. A mancha roxa se estende de Mato Grosso a Goiás e avança por Rondônia, Tocantins e o sul do Pará.

Evangélicos e voto em Flávio Bolsonaro — Foto: Dhara Pereira - Arte/g1

❗ A proporção de pessoas de uma religião em um município não explica sozinha a geografia eleitoral, que se deve a múltiplos fatores que o eleitor pode levar em conta para decidir em quem votar.

A proporção de moradores evangélicos está associada à divisão do voto entre Lula e Flávio no segundo turno, mas essa relação varia bastante pelo país. Quando os municípios são agrupados de acordo com o percentual de evangélicos, a vantagem muda de lado na faixa entre 20% e 40%.

Nos 502 municípios em que os evangélicos representam até 10% da população considerada pelo levantamento, Lula obteve 68,5% dos votos válidos, ante 31,5% de Flávio. Na faixa seguinte, entre 10% e 20% de evangélicos, Lula ainda liderou por 61,3% a 38,7%, considerando 1.929 municípios.

Nos municípios onde mais de 30% da população se declara evangélica, Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) liderou — Foto: Arte/g1

A diferença diminui na faixa de 20% a 30% de população evangélica, formada por 1.819 municípios: Lula aparece com 51,3% dos votos válidos, contra 48,7% de Flávio.

A partir dos 30%, o resultado se inverte. Nos 973 municípios com proporção de evangélicos entre 30% e 40%, Flávio alcançou 54,2% e Lula, 45,8%. Entre 40% e 50%, o placar foi de 54,6% a 45,4%. E nos 58 municípios em que mais da metade da população é evangélica, Flávio chegou a 55,2%, enquanto Lula ficou com 44,8%.

A relação, porém, não se repete com a mesma intensidade em todo o território nacional. O cálculo da correlação entre a proporção municipal de evangélicos e a votação de Lula mostra diferenças entre os estados.

Centro-Oeste: Fé e voto na mesma direção. É onde o padrão aparece com mais nitidez. Goiânia, Campo Grande e Cuiabá têm proporção de evangélicos acima da média nacional, e Flávio venceu com folga nas três. Em Anápolis (GO), onde a presença evangélica é ainda maior, a vantagem do candidato do PL foi ainda mais ampla.

Nordeste: Em 55% dos municípios da região, os evangélicos são proporcionalmente poucos e Flávio teve votação baixa. No outro extremo, o interior nordestino concentra cidades com menos evangélicos e votação expressiva de Lula. Juazeiro do Norte (CE), polo de romarias católicas, é um dos exemplos. Entre as grandes cidades, Salvador e Teresina deram ampla vantagem a Lula.

A região foi o principal reduto de Lula: ainda no primeiro turno, Lula liderou no Nordeste, enquanto Flávio foi melhor no Sudeste, Sul, Centro-Oeste e Norte.

Sul: Flávio é forte mesmo sem evangélicos. Aqui a religião praticamente não explica o voto. Montauri (RS) é a cidade com menor proporção de evangélicos do país e, ainda assim, deu vitória larga a Flávio. O mesmo vale para Caxias do Sul (RS) e Florianópolis (SC), de maioria católica. No mesmo estado fica Arroio do Padre (RS), o município mais evangélico do Brasil, que também votou em peso em Flávio: no Sul, o candidato do PL teve vantagem nos dois extremos.

No Norte acontece o inverso. Em grandes extensões do Amazonas e do Pará, a presença evangélica é alta, mas a votação de Flávio ficou na faixa intermediária ou baixa.

Isso significa que, nesses estados, municípios com percentuais maiores de evangélicos tendem a registrar percentuais menores de votos em Lula. Correlação, no entanto, não demonstra que a religião tenha causado o resultado eleitoral. O indicador mostra que as duas variáveis se movimentam juntas, sem isolar outros fatores que também diferenciam os municípios.

O mapa nacional mostra que a composição religiosa não explica sozinha a geografia eleitoral. Há áreas do Centro-Oeste onde percentuais elevados de evangélicos coincidem com votação elevada em Flávio, enquanto partes do Sul registram força eleitoral de Flávio mesmo sem uma correspondência semelhante entre as duas variáveis.

O mapa reforça o que as pesquisas de intenção de voto já indicavam. No Datafolha feito em 6 e 7 de outubro, logo após o primeiro turno, Flávio tinha 69% de intenção de voto entre os eleitores evangélicos, contra 25% de Lula . Ao contrário do pai, Jair Bolsonaro (PL), que se declara católico, Flávio foi batizado na fé evangélica .

articles.title: Notícias g1 Triângulo: Feminicídio e ofensas de alunos de medicina | G1
articles.standfirst: Resumo de notícias da semana entre os dias 24 e 30 de outubro.
articles.summary: Confira o resumo do g1 Triângulo sobre o feminicídio de Priscila Lacerda, o caso de intolerância na medicina em Araguari e a busca por uma criança em Araxá.
articles.body:
Confira o que foi destaque no g1 Triângulo nesta semana, com as notícias mais acessadas entre os dias 24 a 30 de outubro.

Dois alunos de 19 anos do curso de Medicina do Instituto Master de Ensino Presidente Antônio Carlos (Imepac), em Araguari , são alvo de um processo administrativo disciplinar aberto pela instituição para apurar ofensas a colegas bolsistas em um grupo de WhatsApp. Os áudios foram enviados na noite de domingo (25), após a reeleição do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

Os nomes dos envolvidos não foram divulgados para preservar a identidade das vítimas.

Nas mensagens, os estudantes insultaram colegas que recebem bolsas do Programa Universidade para Todos (Prouni) ou têm financiamento pelo Fundo de Financiamento Estudantil (Fies). Entre os alvos estão alunos que vendem trufas e outros produtos para ajudar a pagar as despesas com os estudos e o custo de vida na cidade.

"Agora quem votou no Lulinha, que está há 20 anos prometendo picanha, quem vier vender trufa [...]. Falar que as minas gostosas que estão com o Lula. Vai todo mundo se f*. Pega a p* da sua bolsa de Prouni, de Fies e divide com a p* do MST", disse um dos estudantes.

Em comunicado publicado nas redes sociais, o Imepac repudiou manifestações de intolerância ou discriminação por convicções políticas ou condição socioeconômica. A instituição informou que abriu um processo para apurar os fatos e avaliar as medidas cabíveis, respeitando as normas internas e o direito de defesa.

A empresária Priscila Lacerda Custodio, que foi morta por um homem 38 anos mais velho, relatou ter sofrido agressões e ameaças quatro dias antes do crime. A jovem tinha 24 anos, era natural de Perdizes , e foi baleada pelo pecuarista João Roberto Bolelli, de 62, em Rifaina (SP), na noite de terça-feira (27).

Priscila viajou cerca de 117 km de Perdizes até a cidade paulista a fim de devolver uma caminhonete do homem que estava com ela e terminar um relacionamento com ele. Ela foi acompanhada pelo irmão e por uma amiga, pois estava apreensiva e havia relatado agressões e ameaças.

Segundo a Polícia Militar (PM), ela encontrou o pecuarista às margens da Rodovia Cândido Portinari (SP-334), próximo a uma propriedade rural. No local, houve uma discussão entre os dois envolvendo um celular que ele teria dado a ela.

O irmão da vítima contou à polícia que a jovem disse que queria ir embora e não desejava continuar o relacionamento. Durante o desentendimento, Bolelli sacou uma arma e atirou contra Priscila. Ele fugiu após o crime e é investigado por feminicídio.

Uma menina de 11 anos foi encontrada escondida em uma igreja 20 horas após ser dada como desaparecida em Araxá , no sábado (24). A menina voltava para casa quando perdeu os óculos na rua e se perdeu.

Segundo o delegado responsável pelo caso, Jeferson Leal da Silva, o desaparecimento foi comunicado às 18h da sexta-feira (23), após ela sair da casa de uma amiga. A criança encontrou a igreja após se perder e entrou sem ser percebida.

O espaço estava aberto para uma missa, mas poucas pessoas estavam presentes. Ela se escondeu em uma cozinha e passou a noite inteira ali.

Segundo a Polícia Civil, a menina estava muito assustada e ficou escondida o tempo todo. A igreja foi trancada após a missa sem ninguém perceber a presença dela. Na cozinha, ela se alimentou de bolachas e fez uma "cama" no chão com roupas que encontrou no local.

Conforme o delegado, ela ainda trocou de roupa com as peças que achou. No dia seguinte, a igreja foi reaberta, ainda sem ninguém ver a menina. Por volta das 14h de sábado (24), as polícias Civil e Militar foram até a igreja e encontraram a menina escondida.

articles.title: Novo segue sem reconhecer resultado das eleições; 27 partidos validam vitória de Lula | G1
articles.standfirst: Enquanto o PL, partido de Flávio Bolsonaro, reconheceu o resultado das eleições no último dia 25, o partido Novo segue sem reconhecer o veredito das urnas na eleição presidencial.
articles.summary: Enquanto o PL, partido de Flávio Bolsonaro, reconheceu o resultado das eleições no último dia 25, o partido Novo segue sem reconhecer o veredito das urnas na eleição presidencial.
articles.body:
Logo após o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) proclamar Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) vencedor da disputa com o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), por uma diferença de 4,4 milhões de votos, o presidente do partido Novo , Eduardo Ribeiro, não reconheceu o resultado das urnas e afirmou que "o Brasil não vive uma democracia".

Ao todos, vinte e sete partidos políticos divulgaram manifestações em que reconhecem a vitória do presidente Lula nas eleições deste ano . Até a última atualização desta reportagem, apenas uma legenda não havia se manifestado sobre o resultado das eleições: Mobiliza.

Em uma publicação nas redes sociais, Ribeiro questionou o resultado alegando uso da máquina pública e do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), em uma referência a decisão do ministro Cristiano Zanin, que prorrogou o período de votação até às 19h, pedido que havia sido feito também pelo PL.

“O resultado da eleição é a prova de que o Brasil não é uma democracia. Como se não bastasse fazer uma campanha cheia de mentiras, o PT usou como nunca a máquina pública e o STF pra se manter no poder. Temos três ações pedindo a cassação da chapa de Lula. Cabe agora à Justiça cumprir seu papel, se ainda existe Justiça nesse país”, afirmou o presidente do partido.

O Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) atestou a regularidade do processo eleitoral e reconheceu a vitória do presidente Lula ainda no domingo (25), após a totalização dos votos. Após o resultado, Flávio disse não reconhecer a vitória de Lula e afirmou que iria pedir a anulação da votação .

Depois da divulgação da carta de Flávio, questionando o resultado nas urnas, o presidente da Corte Eleitoral, ministro Kassio Nunes Marques, indicado ao cargo de ministro do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) pelo ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL), afirmou que a Justiça Eleitoral entregou o pleito deste ano com segurança e que as eleições "transcorreram dentro da mais absoluta normalidade".

Entre as siglas que reconheceram a vitória estão o PL — partido do candidato derrotado Flávio Bolsonaro —, União Brasil, MDB, PSD, Republicanos, PSDB, PDT, PSB, PSOL, Podemos, Avante, Democrata, Democracia Cristã (DC), UP e PSTU .

27 partidos reconheceram vitória de Lula nas urnas — Foto: Reprodução/Jornal Nacional

Ao g1, Ribeiro afirmou que o partido continuará sem reconhecer o resultado das eleições presidenciais por uma questão de coerência.

“Não vai mudar. Primeiro porque seria contraditório a gente reconhecer a vitória de uma chapa que a gente ainda está contestando na Justiça. O Novo tem três ações contra a chapa Lula-Alckmin, todas elas ajuizadas antes da eleição”, declarou Ribeiro.

Questionado se o partido mudará o posicionamento caso seja derrotado na Justiça, Ribeiro afirmou que o partido irá avaliar “a decisão e os argumentos”.

O partido também não se manifestou sobre a carta escrita por Flávio Bolsonaro após fugir do país para os Estados Unidos em que o candidato derrotado, em tom golpista, se autoproclamou presidente eleito do país, voltando atrás minutos depois e trocando a expressão por “líder do Brasil”.

Apesar de não ter se posicionado, Ribeiro diz que o partido deixou os quadros “livres para cada um se posicionar” e afirmou que, apesar de não reconhecer, o Novo não questiona a lisura das urnas e do pleito.

“Em nenhum momento a gente questionou as urnas. Nós estamos questionando os meios ilegais, no nosso entendimento, que o Lula usou. Por ser um incumbente, por estar na administração pública, por ter a caneta na mão, que fizeram com que a eleição não fosse justa”, pontuou.

Segundo o g1 apurou, a postura é parte de uma estratégia do partido que está apostando em “um racha” da direita, principalmente no PL, entre abraçar ou não o discurso golpista de Flávio Bolsonaro de não reconhecer o resultado das eleições presidenciais.

Buscando atrair esses quadros, o Novo deve continuar não reconhecendo a vitória de Lula.

Questionado, Ribeiro disse que não há uma estratégia, que o partido não irá entrar em eventuais disputas dentro da direita, mas que está “de portas abertas” para receber quadros da direita que se identifiquem com a legenda.

“O Novo vai estar de portas abertas a todos aqueles que consideram o Novo como um partido de direita, liberal, conservador, que tem princípios, que tem pessoas decentes. O Novo vai estar sempre de portas aberta, mas nós não temos interesse em entrar em rusgas da direita nesse momento”, afirmou.

Presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) durante ato de campanha em São Paulo — Foto: Ricardo Stuckert

O Novo já havia sinalizado ao bolsonarismo durante a campanha presidencial do ex-governador de Minas Gerais, Romeu Zema.

Após a revelação dos áudios em que Flávio Bolsonaro pede e cobra dinheiro de Daniel Vorcaro , então dono do Banco Master, para bancar o filme "Dark Horse", sobre a vida do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, Zema foi um dos primeiros políticos a criticar a relação entre o senador e o banqueiro.

“Flávio Bolsonaro, ouvir você cobrando dinheiro do Vorcaro é imperdoável. É um tapa na cara dos brasileiros de bem. Não adianta nada criticar as práticas de Lula e do PT e fazer a mesma coisa”, declarou à época.

As declarações não caíram bem dentro do partido e Zema foi cobrado por correligionários a baixar o tom contra Flávio para não atrapalhar palanques locais, como Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina e Paraná.

Zema então passou a falar em união da direita “para derrotar o PT”, mas acabou abandonado por quadros do partido ainda no primeiro turno.

Um deles foi Marcel Van Hattem, deputado que acabou eleito senador pelo Rio Grande do Sul. A três dias do primeiro turno, o parlamentar declarou em live realizada com Flávio Bolsonaro que “no domingo votaria 22”.

Nas eleições, o Novo elegeu dez deputados federais, três senadores e rompeu a cláusula de barreira.

🔎 Também chamada de cláusula de desempenho, a regra estabelece que os partidos precisam atingir um percentual mínimo de votos válidos para a Câmara dos Deputados ou um número mínimo de deputados eleitos para ter acesso a recursos do Fundo Partidário e ao tempo de propaganda na televisão e no rádio.

Romeu Zema acabou na sexta colocação com apenas 326.488 votos, 0,27% dos votos válidos. A performance foi pior que a de Felipe D’Avila, candidato do partido em 2022, que foi votado por 559.708 eleitores, 0,47% do total.

articles.body:
Ukraine gets approval for Patriot missile sale

The State Department approved on Friday a possible $2.1 billion sale of 500 Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine that is funded entirely by U.S. partners and allies.

The Trump administration greenlit the sale of 500 PATRIOT Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE) missiles, including classified and unclassified spare parts

“This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe,” the State Department said in the press release.

Ukraine will pay for the purchase with donations from Norway, Germany and Canada via the JUMPSTART program and national funds. No U.S. funds are involved in the transaction.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said that Patriot missile interceptors are paramount to shooting down Russian missiles and drones targeting the country’s cities.

Zelensky has previously accused the Pentagon of delaying deliveries of missile interceptors that other nations bought for Kyiv.

“We have been waiting for nearly a month for Mr. Hegseth to sign off on missiles for Patriots and NASAMS,” Zelensky said this week .

Two weeks ago, Hegseth told reporters that the Pentagon has not changed its posture toward Ukraine, but noted that “we want to make sure our guys have the most possible” interceptors.

articles.title: Judge orders DOJ to stop threatening to prosecute election officials
articles.summary: The San Francisco-based court also said federal officials must stop demanding that ballots from selected voters be segregated.
articles.body:
A federal judge on Friday ordered the Justice Department to stop threatening state and local election officials with criminal prosecution over their handling of disputes about voter qualifications.

U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson also ordered the Trump administration to cease demanding that election workers remove voters from statewide rolls, refuse to issue ballots to specific voters or segregate ballots cast in the midterms based on the administration's claims that some voters are ineligible.

"Because the public has a paramount interest in ensuring that election officials and workers are able to carry out their work in accordance with federal law and election procedure, and the official day of the Elections is only a couple of days away, the balance of the equities and public interest weigh in Plaintiffs' favor," Thompson wrote.

Thompson, a San Francisco-based Biden appointee, issued the temporary restraining order in connection with a lawsuit brought by the Service Employees International Union and other groups. Her directive also requires the DOJ to reach out to any state or local officials who received warnings about possible prosecution and inform them that "demands and threats of prosecution to election officials and workers … have been enjoined."

The Justice Department on Thursday sent letters to election workers in all 50 states alluding to possible prosecution if they didn't preserve election records. DOJ did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the judge's broad ruling.

Thompson's order effectively enforces a stern warning issued to the Trump administration by another California-based federal judge, David Carter, earlier this week. "These threats must stop," Carter wrote in a ruling that threw out the Justice Department's effort to compel California to set aside any ballots cast by up to 20,000 people federal officials had identified as likely noncitizens. The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals on Friday declined to set aside Carter's order.

Thompson's new directive also follows an order by U.S. District Judge James Boasberg, chief of the federal district court in Washington, D.C., to require the Trump administration to provide the list of those 20,000 purported noncitizens to an immigrant advocacy group. Boasberg's order was rooted, in part, on the group's claim that the Trump administration's threats were influencing the conduct of state and local elected officials.

articles.title: Judge orders Trump administration to stop threatening election officials with criminal charges
articles.summary: A federal judge issued a sweeping order blocking the Trump administration from threatening or intimidating election officials amid pressure tactics used by the administration in the weeks leading up to next week’s midterm elections.
articles.body: A federal judge issued a sweeping order Friday night blocking the Trump administration from threatening or intimidating election officials amid pressure tactics used by the administration in the weeks leading up to the Nov. 3 midterm elections. The eight-page order prohibits any action that may “threaten, intimidate or coerce state or local elections officials or workers to demand that they halt processing the ballots of any registered voter solely on the basis that the ballot belongs to an individual alleged by [the administration] to be ineligible to vote.” U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson, who’s based in California, wrote, “In the lead-up to the election, high-ranking DOJ and DHS officials have engaged in a campaign to intimidate, threaten, and coerce state and local officials and employees who are engaged in administering the ongoing midterm 2026 election.” The order comes in the wake of efforts to require states like California and Washington to separate out ballots the administration says could be cast by noncitizens. An appeals court ruled against the administration in California this week; the Washington case is pending. “Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters,” Thompson wrote Friday. The judge’s order extends through Nov. 16, nearly two weeks after Election Day. The Justice Department sent letters to election officials in 57 of California’s 58 counties last week, directing them to cooperate with the DOJ’s investigations of illegal voting or face investigations themselves. “As you’re aware, federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections,” a letter sent to an election official in San Bernardino County on Oct. 22 said. “I write to seek your help to protect the integrity of the ongoing federal election.” First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bilal Essayli wrote in the letter that he was attaching a list of “1133 likely aliens” registered to vote in San Bernardino County. “Within 48 hours, we ask that you commit to working with DOJ and DHS to identify who on the accompanying list is a citizen and who is not,” Essayli wrote, adding, “That means sending us the nonpublic information associated with each suspected alien’s registration,” including Social Security numbers, state IDs or driver’s licenses. “For individuals whom citizenship status cannot be confirmed, we request that you immediately instruct the appropriate elections official to segregate—not cancel—those individuals’ vote-by-mail ballots until their citizenship status can be determined,” Essayli wrote. Essayli asserted that the list of alleged noncitizens was created by a “multilayered, multiagency investigative methodology” by DHS. He urged the election officials to comply, reiterating that “The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring federal crimes are significant.” In a Friday ruling, a federal appeals court rejected the Trump administration’s request to force California election officials to segregate ballots that it says are from noncitizens. The decision followed a separate ruling from a federal appeals court Monday to also deny the DOJ’s bid to block more than 20,000 ballots from being counted over claims of noncitizens being on the state’s voter rolls. And Wednesday, a federal judge argued that the Justice Department’s request to segregate the ballots “violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,” and questioned the administration’s processes for identifying the alleged noncitizens.
