articles.title: Haley Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed clash over Israel ad ahead of planned rally together
articles.summary: The tensions between the former Democratic primary candidates have drawn in other Michigan Democrats as the party hopes to secure a critical Senate seat.
articles.body: Days before they are set to headline a rally in Detroit, Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., traded critical messages in statements released Friday, escalating tensions between the two in the final stretch of El-Sayed’s campaign for Senate. Stevens said that she expected El-Sayed, the progressive candidate who defeated her in a bitter Democratic primary in August, to formally condemn an ad from an outside progressive group that she called antisemitic, adding that it’s why she agreed to join El-Sayed on the campaign trail for the first time on Sunday. “This ad tells Michigan families they cannot afford groceries because their money has to be set aside for ‘killing Palestinians,’ and it blames our close ally Israel for everything Michiganders cannot afford,” Stevens said in a statement. She sought to tie the ad — which is set in a grocery store and suggests Israel and the war in Gaza are to blame for rising prices in America — to comments El-Sayed has made in his own campaign. “I therefore expect him to apologize for those statements as well,” Stevens said. “Abdul promises to get money out of politics. He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.” El-Sayed is not affiliated with the group that produced the ad, Rebellion PAC, and his campaign distanced itself from the ad in statements to The New York Times earlier this week. Stevens also called on El-Sayed to take down one of his own ads that featured right-wing commentator Tucker Carlson “out of the same respect for Michigan’s Black community.” El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel, shot back Friday, saying in a statement that Stevens, a strong supporter of Israel, “seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago” and that his campaign’s focus was on affordability and health care. “That focus is why our people-powered campaign defeated a historic $70M in outside spending from big corporations and AIPAC on behalf of Congresswoman Stevens,” El-Sayed said, referencing Stevens’ support from the American Israeli Public Affairs Committee, a pro-Israel lobbying group, during the primary. The exchange comes after the former primary opponents had seemingly reached a reconciliation, agreeing to appear at an event in Detroit alongside senior Democratic leader Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., on Sunday. The escalation is also playing out four days before voters will choose between El-Sayed and Republican candidate Mike Rogers to be the next Michigan senator in a race the nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates as a toss-up. It’s unclear whether Stevens’ and El-Sayed’s Friday statements will affect their appearance Sunday. Representatives for Stevens and El-Sayed did not respond when asked for additional comment and whether the two still planned to appear at the event. On Wednesday, Stevens sat for an interview on CNN in which she signaled she would vote for El-Sayed while also calling on him to denounce the ad from Rebellion PAC. That interview came shortly after Stevens’ fiancé, Jason Turkish, told The Detroit News that he was voting for Rogers. “Of course I’m voting for our Democratic nominee for Senate,” Stevens said. “I’m voting for the Democratic ticket. But I want to encourage this campaign to shut out the hate and to call it out and to make people who are in my coalition, make them feel comfortable about coming to the polls.” The tensions between El-Sayed and Stevens have drawn in other Michigan Democrats as the party hopes to secure a critical Senate seat in the race to control Congress. “First of all, I have no idea what the hell Haley Stevens is doing,” Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow said Friday on CNN. “This is a moment where we have to recognize the stakes.” Democratic Rep. Debbie Dingell, a senior member of Michigan’s delegation, sought to downplay the conflict on NBC News’ “Meet the Press NOW,” saying Friday that she helped broker the event Sunday with Clyburn, who is close with Stevens. “I think that, quite frankly, a lot of people are trying to create more controversy here, when I think the real discussion should be about what’s been happening in Washington and how we’ve got to stand up to what we’ve seen in the last two years,” Dingell said.

articles.title: Judge blocks DOJ from threatening election officials over noncitizen voting claims
articles.summary: A California federal judge Friday ordered the Trump administration to stop threatening election officials with criminal prosecution in its ongoing efforts to crack down on noncitizen voting. U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson issued a temporary restraining order connected to a lawsuit brought by unions representing California election workers earlier Friday. In her decision, the Biden-appointed judge…
articles.body:
A California federal judge Friday ordered the Trump administration to stop threatening election officials with criminal prosecution in its ongoing efforts to crack down on noncitizen voting.

U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson issued a temporary restraining order connected to a lawsuit brought by unions representing California election workers earlier Friday. In her decision, the Biden-appointed judge noted Election Day was “around the corner.”

“Ballots have already been issued. Americans have already begun voting. Workers have already begun processing ballots,” Thompson wrote. “Given the consequences of inaction, the Court sees no reason to delay its ruling.”

The order also directs the Trump administration to halt its efforts to force these workers to remove certain people from voter rolls, deny ballot requests to some voters or set aside ballots for individuals it suspects are ineligible to vote.

The plaintiffs involved in this case include The Service Employees International Union; American Federation Of State, County and Municipal Employees; the League Of United Latin American Citizens and the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People.

The initial complaint accuses Attorney General Todd Blanche and other top Justice Department (DOJ) officials of carrying out “a coordinated campaign to intimidate, threaten, and coerce state and local officials and employees.”

This week, the DOJ sent letters to election officials in all 50 states threatening potential prosecution if they failed to preserve election records.

The DOJ had sent similar correspondence a week prior to election officials in every California county, demanding they work with the federal government to identify potential noncitizens on their voter rolls. The letter warned these officials would “risk significant federal scrutiny” if they failed to comply with this request.

Earlier this week, another federal judge in California threw out the Trump administration’s lawsuit attempting to require the state to set aside the ballots of 20,000 people the federal government had identified as potential noncitizens. A split federal appeals court panel upheld this ruling Friday.

The Hill has reached out to the DOJ and the White House for comment on Thompson’s order.

articles.body:
Democrats running for Senate in Maine, Alaska and New Hampshire are zeroing in on the rising cost of home heating as winter — and Election Day — quickly approach.

Republican candidates have been on defense in key Senate battlegrounds, arguing against the claim that the GOP has enabled President Trump’s war in Iran, which has inflated oil costs. The cost of residential heating oil went from an average of less than $4 per gallon before the war to more than $6 today.

“There are a lot of people here who are stretched pretty thin, and home heating costs are an issue even during the best of times,” said Mark Brewer, the chair of the political science department at the University of Maine.

“So when we’re talking about a spike like this, it’s a huge issue,” he continued.

Democrats are narrowly favored to flip the Senate, according to Decision Desk HQ, as Republicans confront voter anger over high costs due to the Iran war. The Republicans running for Senate in Maine, New Hampshire and Alaska either declined to comment for this story or did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

Democrats’ path to a Senate majority may run through Maine, a state where about half of homes use heating oil to stay warm. Democrat Troy Jackson has sought to assign blame to his opponent, Republican Sen. Susan Collins (Maine).

“Unlike Susan Collins, Troy understands what it’s like to worry about the furnace shutting off in the middle of the night and in the U.S. Senate, he’ll fight to lower costs and end the war in Iran that’s only making it harder for Mainers to make ends meet,” campaign spokesperson Ella McFarlane told The Hill in a statement.

The Collins campaign referred The Hill to a campaign webpage highlighting the senator’s opposition to the conflict and vote to halt military actions despite initially opposing efforts to halt the war. The website does not reference heating oil.

Energy costs are just one example of the larger trend of rising costs nationwide. Seventy-five percent of U.S. adults report seeing higher energy costs in recent years, and 84 percent of registered voters surveyed by Pew Research Center said the economy is important to their vote.

Collins pushed the Trump administration in September to address the cost of heating oil this fall.

“It now costs about $675 more to fill a standard tank than it did last year — a significant hardship for the half of Maine households that heat their homes with fuel oil,” Collins wrote in a letter to President Trump, urging him to release oil from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve.

The administration then released 315,000 barrels of heating oil, though it’s unclear how much relief that will provide to consumers. It’s among a blitz of announcements from Collins in recent months either criticizing Trump or flexing her ability to influence decisions in Washington.

James Melcher, political science professor at the University of Maine at Farmington, said the home heating issue will reinforce how voters already feel about the candidates.

Jackson voters blame Trump and Collins for high costs while Collins voters — and Collins herself — blame Democrats and the Maine Legislature, Melcher said.

New Hampshire’s Chris Pappas, a House Democrat running for Senate, has called on fellow legislators to authorize additional funding and for full distribution of the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP). LIHEAP aids nearly 6 million homes nationwide in affording energy costs.

“Granite Staters deserve a fighter who is focused on lowering costs, delivering relief, and putting New Hampshire first — not rubber-stamping an agenda that leaves working families footing the bill,” Pappas said in a statement to The Hill.

Republican John Sununu, a former senator from the Granite State, has said he would support increased LIHEAP funding, a cause also championed by Collins. He has also called for infrastructure development to further improve energy costs, while criticizing Trump for entering the Iran war without a plan to keep the Strait of Hormuz, a key shipping route for oil, open for passage.

Melcher said New Hampshire’s GOP governor likely prevents Sununu from blaming the state government for high costs like Collins can.

In Alaska, Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) is running a tight race for reelection in a state where gas and oil costs have reached double digits in some communities. Sullivan has called for a diesel export moratorium to help ease costs and said at an October rally that high costs are a “small price to pay” to prevent a nuclear Iran.

“The conflict in the Middle East is temporary,” Sullivan said. “The true forever war is the national Democrats’ war against Alaska oil and gas and our jobs. That’s the forever war.”

Former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska), the Democratic candidate running against Sullivan, has pinned the blame squarely on his support of Trump’s agenda, warning Alaskans are worried people will freeze to death because they will have to chose between paying for food or warmth this winter.

“Mary will stand up to anyone to take on DC corruption, lower costs, and put Alaska first – and Dan Sullivan will be forced to answer for raising costs on Alaskans this November,” a spokesperson for the Peltola campaign told The Hill.

Alexander Hirsch, chair of the political science department at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, said Alaskan voters have often swung with the economy. He said energy costs are a perennial issue, and while Alaskans may point the finger at different people for the rising cost of oil, voters seem to want change.

“Some Alaskan voters are blaming tariffs, others have a different scapegoat, but I think the bottom line is that Alaskans want to see a change in a political representation in order to bring about an impactful change in terms of their everyday lives,” Hirsch said.

articles.title: 5 races that will tell the story of the midterms
articles.summary: A dramatic midterm campaign is in its final days. There have been internal party tensions, deeply controversial ads, and, famously, two Dan Sullivans in Alaska’s Senate race. At the center of everything, of course, is President Trump. A House majority is widely assumed to be within Democrats’ grasp. The Hill’s data and polling partner, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ),…
articles.body:
A dramatic midterm campaign is in its final days.

There have been internal party tensions , deeply controversial ads , and, famously, two Dan Sullivans in Alaska’s Senate race. At the center of everything , of course, is President Trump.

A House majority is widely assumed to be within Democrats’ grasp. The Hill’s data and polling partner, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), gives the opposition party an 82 percent chance of prevailing, as of Friday. The Senate is a much closer battle, though DDHQ gives Democrats a 62 percent edge there, too.

Beyond the math, some key races will tell a broader story about where politics stands in 2026. Here are five of them.

Texas should be safe Republican territory given that Trump carried the Lone Star State by 13 points over Democratic nominee Kamala Harris two years ago. But it is anything but safe — and Trump will bear some blame if the GOP candidate goes down.

Trump never seemed particularly enamored of incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R), who the president felt had been insufficiently supportive. In 2023, as Trump sought to win the GOP nomination for the following year’s election, Cornyn contended “Trump’s time has passed him by.”

Cornyn would later try to stay as close to Trump as possible, but it wasn’t enough. The president endorsed Cornyn’s primary opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, in the final stretch of their contest.

Paxton won the primary by almost 30 points. But polls show him struggling against his Democratic opponent, 37-year-old state Rep. James Talarico. In the DDHQ polling average , Talarico is up by almost 4 points.

A loss in Texas would be a crushing blow for the GOP.

If it happens, Trump’s backing of Paxton — whose history includes settling securities fraud charges, messy divorce proceedings, and an impeachment by the Texas House — will come under a harsher microscope.

Michigan Senate: Israel and Islam become central

Abdul El-Sayed is the standard-bearer for the left of the Democratic Party on Tuesday.

That’s not only because of his advocacy of “Medicare for All” or his other signature goal of reducing the influence of corporate money in politics.

It’s also because his fate is inextricably tied to his views of Israel and to the Michigan electorate’s attitudes toward Islam.

El-Sayed, born in Michigan to Egyptian parents, would be the first Muslim senator in U.S. history. He has also been vigorously critical of Israel’s conduct, especially in Gaza, which he deems a genocide.

The Israel question was central to his primary battle with Rep. Haley Stevens (D).

El-Sayed prevailed despite groups affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee spending about $30 million to back Stevens. Tensions remain high on the question, not least given Stevens’s highly unusual statement Friday, when she said she would appear alongside El-Sayed on Sunday but also demanded he apologize for some of his rhetoric.

El-Sayed and his supporters don’t believe he has any reason to apologize. On Friday, the candidate jabbed back at Stevens, accusing her of being “intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.”

In the general election, El-Sayed has been on the receiving end of Islamophobic attacks from Trump, who has called him a “jihadist” on several occasions and has also said that he is “on the side of the terrorists.”

El-Sayed has influential allies, too, however. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) said in mid-October she had transferred $1 million from her coffers to his.

El-Sayed leads his GOP opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers (Mich.), by almost 5 points in the DDHQ average.

His result on Tuesday, whatever way it goes, will send a loud message to the rest of his party.

Ohio governor: Ad furor overshadows all else

The polls suggest a tight race in Ohio to take over from Gov. Mike DeWine (R), who is term limited.

But that’s not why the contest between Republican Vivek Ramaswamy and Democrat Amy Acton has seized the public imagination.

Rather, it’s all about an ad. In the final stretch, the Ramaswamy campaign created an ad in which Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, called her daughter a “liar.”

But that wasn’t even half the story. The highly unusual ad brought the spotlight back to Acton’s traumatic childhood.

In summary, Acton suffered a highly unstable upbringing, and her stepfather was charged with sexually abusing her. The stepfather, Cledith Arthur, pleaded his innocence but skipped the state to avoid trial — and Donna Arthur stayed with him. Cledith Arthur died in 2004.

The ad was massively controversial and was condemned even by some Republicans, including DeWine and his predecessor as governor, John Kasich. Trump, however, defended it, as did Ramaswamy.

The DDHQ polling average showed Acton ahead by less than 3 points as of Friday.

Maine Senate: GOP moderate gets assist from Democratic turmoil

In a year when GOP Senate seats in conservative strongholds like Texas and Kansas look to be in danger, Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) should be doomed. Trump lost Maine by 7 points to Harris in 2024.

Collins is down just 3.5 points to Democratic opponent Troy Jackson, a former state senator, in the DDHQ average. She has outperformed the polls before, as when she won a reelection race she was expected to lose six years ago.

If she survives, it will partly be down to her ability to brand herself as willing to buck Trump — even though Democrats have long argued her much-vaunted “independence” is overstated.

Collins has also been given an assist by Democratic turmoil.

Initially, oyster farmer Graham Platner, running as a populist, vanquished the Democratic Party establishment’s choice, Gov. Janet Mills. But Platner faced a blizzard of controversies, including a tattoo associated with the Nazis, before things reached their nadir with an allegation of rape. Platner denied wrongdoing but withdrew from the race in July.

Jackson is generally seen as a solid but uninspiring campaigner.

The question is whether the state’s Democratic lean will carry Jackson over the finish line or whether the wily Collins can eke out a win yet again.

South Carolina Senate: What’s in a name?

Theoretically, an incumbent Republican senator in South Carolina should be safe. The state backed Trump by 18 points in 2024.

But this is a highly unusual race. Sen. Darline Graham (R) has been in office only since July, when she was appointed by the state’s governor to replace her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), after his sudden death.

The new senator has not exactly wowed with her performance. The most startling example came during an August debate when she said she was not “that informed on national security” and that the subject “is not my thing.”

Graham faces an unexpectedly strong challenge from Democrat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who holds centrist positions on topics like immigration. Trump has sometimes attacked her using a slur for trans people, though Andrews is not trans.

The DDHQ polling average has the race essentially tied, with Graham up just one-tenth of a point.

The political complexion of South Carolina makes many observers think Graham might hold on in the end. A GOP loss in the Palmetto State would be seismic.

articles.title: Can Democrats win the US Senate? 10 key midterm races to watch
articles.summary: From Texas to Maine, rising prices and the Iran war put key Senate races in play as Democrats fight for control.
articles.body:
Democrats need a net gain of at least four seats in November’s midterm elections to take control of the United States Senate from Republicans, as voter discontent with President Donald Trump, the Iran war, and rising prices heighten the races in once-safe Republican states.

Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, and a Democratic takeover seemed highly unlikely at the start of the year – before the US launched its war on Iran.

Here are the key races that could decide the control of the Senate:

Republican Senator Dan Sullivan is seeking re-election against Democratic former US Representative Mary Peltola and an independent candidate who shares Sullivan’s name.

Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, allowing voters to rank candidates in order of preference. Four candidates are on the ballot, including Sullivan, Peltola and another Dan Sullivan , a candidate Republicans accuse Democrats of recruiting deliberately to confuse voters.

“It was a scheme. It was election fraud. Total election fraud,” Trump said. Peltola has rejected the accusations, saying the dispute is distracting from voters’ concerns.

“I feel like this is yet another diversion from the issue that Alaskans want to talk about, which is affordability,” she explained.

Peltola has raised $33m in October, compared with nearly $14m for Sullivan. Republicans have also spent more on the race, $42m compared with $38m by Democrats.

Trump won Alaska by 13 points in 2024, but recent opinion polls suggest Peltola narrowly leading over Sullivan.

Iowa has been a Republican stronghold in recent elections, with Trump winning the state by 13 points in 2024. But his declining popularity, trade tariffs and the Iran war have put Republicans on the defence in Iowa.

The state’s agricultural economy has been hit hard by trade tariffs as well as rising fuel and fertiliser costs as a result of the strained oil supplies amid the Iran war.

Republican US Senator Joni Ernst’s decision not to seek re-election has left an open-seat contest between Republican US Representative Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Representative Josh Turek, a two-time Paralympic gold medallist.

Republican Hinson has called for an “immediate end” to the Iran war and said Iowans should not have to pay higher fuel or grocery prices as a result of it. However, according to Politifact , Hinson has voted against six resolutions seeking to end US involvement in the Iran war.

Turek has outraised Hinson $20m to $14m, but recent polls show Hinson with a narrow lead.

Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, but rising farming costs, opposition to Trump’s immigration crackdown and discontent over the Iran war have made this year’s race unexpectedly competitive.

Trump won the state by 16 percentage points in 2024.

Republican Senator Roger Marshall is facing Democrat Adam Hamilton, the founding pastor of a Methodist megachurch.

The race has drawn attention from Republican leaders, with both Trump and Vice President JD Vance campaigning in the state.

Agriculture is central to Kansas’s economy, and farmers have struggled with rising diesel and fertiliser prices as a result of the Iran war. Many have also expressed frustration with Trump’s tariffs.

Immigration has become another major issue. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids in southwest Kansas have disrupted businesses. Even Republican Marshall has criticised aspects of the agency’s operations in his state.

Democrat Hamilton has outraised Marshall, $14m to $6m. Democratic groups have also outspent Republicans in Kansas, $28m to $22m.

Recent polls show Hamilton narrowly ahead.

Maine is one of the Democrats’ biggest opportunities to gain a Senate seat, as Republican Senator Susan Collins faces a close re-election battle in a state which voted against Donald Trump in 2024.

Collins faces Democrat Troy Jackson, a former Maine Senate president who entered the race in July after the party’s original nominee, Graham Platner, withdrew following sexual assault allegations, which he denied.

Collins has sought to distance herself from Trump, acknowledging during a debate earlier this month that she was not the president’s favourite senator and that he would not be campaigning in Maine.

She was among the Republicans who voted to convict Trump following his impeachment over the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol.

Democrats say Collins only votes against Trump when it doesn’t matter, however. Democrats also hope voters will hold her accountable for helping confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the US Supreme Court, which led to the overturning of a federal right to abortion.

Jackson has faced criticism over his treatment of women, including his refusal to apologise for telling Collins to “shut up” during a debate.

Jackson has outraised Collins, bringing in about $26.9m compared with $25.2m through mid-October. Republican groups have also outspent Democrats, $76m to $40m.

Republicans appear to have conceded North Carolina , where even Trump has suggested the Democrats will win. At a campaign rally last week in Greenville, Trump told supporters it was “crazy” that former Governor Roy Cooper, a Democrat, was going to be their next senator.

Trump won North Carolina by 3 points in 2024, but Republican Senator Thom Tillis’ retirement made this year’s Senate race an open contest.

Trump recruited former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley to succeed Tillis, but he has been unable to compete with Cooper’s fundraising, and Republican allies who invested heavily in holding North Carolina ‌have begun shifting their focus ⁠to other states.

Affordability has dominated the campaign as farmers struggle with rising diesel and energy costs amid the Iran war.

In eastern North Carolina, Kelly Spivey, who runs a community food pantry, told Al Jazeera that rising prices are forcing families to make difficult choices.

“They’re trying to decide if they’re going to pay for their medicine or they’re going to buy food or they’re going to pay for day care so they can actually go to work,” she said.

Whatley, meanwhile, has closely aligned himself with Trump, who told supporters at a campaign rally: “I just want you to go out and pretend I’m on the ticket because essentially I am.”

Cooper has raised $50m and has $9m in the bank. Whatley has raised $14m and has just $900,000 on hand through mid-October. Recent polls have Cooper leading by double digits.

Democrat Sherrod Brown, who has longstanding ties to labour unions and working-class communities, is seeking to win back voters in the industrial Rust Belt state.

Brown faces US Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to the Senate to replace US Vice President JD Vance when Vance left the Senate for the White House.

The cost of living has become a major campaign issue.

The winner of the special election will be on the ballot again in 2028 for a full six-year term.

Republican and Democratic outside groups have each spent nine figures on the race, with Republicans investing $232m and Democrats pouring in $118m.

Brown has more than tripled Husted’s fundraising through October 14, bringing in $68m to Husted’s nearly $20m. Recent polls show Brown leading by three to five points.

No Democrat has won statewide in Texas since 1994.

James Talarico, a state representative, could break the streak.

Talarico faces Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton.

Trump won Texas by nearly 14 points in 2024. Yet Republican outside groups have already spent $300m to hold the seat after run-off voters nominated the scandal-plagued Paxton over ⁠incumbent Republican US Senator John Cornyn.

Trump endorsed Paxton even though Cornyn was widely believed to have an easier path to victory.

Leaked audio has exposed daylight between Trump and Paxton, who privately told donors that the president’s midterm convention hurt his campaign.

Democratic groups have spent $76m on this race. But Talarico’s campaign has outraised Paxton’s by $110m and reported $9.6m more in its campaign coffers as of September 30.

Musk has given $158m to a Republican super PAC to invest in Paxton’s race. Recent polls show Talarico narrowly leading or tied.

Georgia was initially seen as one of the Republicans’ main opportunities to gain a Senate seat after Trump won the state by 2 percentage points in 2024. But Republican US Representative Mike Collins has struggled to gain traction against Democratic US Senator Jon Ossoff, a potential 2028 presidential candidate.

Ossoff has ⁠outraised Collins by nearly $126m up to October 14 and began mid-October with $15.1m in his war chest, compared with Collins’ $1.1m.

Polls have consistently shown Ossoff leading, and Democrats narrowly lead Republicans in outside spending, $19m to $17.9m.

Republicans are more hopeful about flipping an open seat in Michigan , especially after the Democratic establishment failed to get its pick nominated.

Progressive outsider Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated centrist US Representative Haley Stevens during the primary, putting him on a collision course with Republican Mike Rogers, a former US representative, in what could be the tightest race for a Democratic-held Senate seat this year.

Michigan, a key battleground state which Trump won in 2024, has been hit by tariffs affecting trade with neighbouring Canada and rising living costs, making the economy a central issue in the campaign.

The race has also attracted heavy spending from outside groups. A pro-Israel super PAC has spent at least $493,000 opposing El-Sayed, after spending $30m in an unsuccessful effort to prevent him from winning the Democratic nomination. The group could spend as much as $9m more during the general election.

El-Sayed raised $45m up to September, more than double Rogers’s nearly $21m.

Republican groups have spent $136m on the race, compared with about $70m by Democrats.

Most recent polls show El-Sayed narrowly ahead.

Democrats are defending an open Senate seat in New Hampshire after Senator Jeanne Shaheen announced her retirement, giving Republicans an opportunity to compete in a state Kamala Harris won by nearly three percentage points in 2024.

Democratic US Representative Chris Pappas faces former Republican Senator John Sununu, who is seeking a return to Washington nearly two decades after losing his seat to Shaheen in 2008.

Sununu comes from one of New Hampshire’s best-known political families. His brother, Chris Sununu, served as governor until 2025.

Pappas has a substantial fundraising advantage, raising $24m compared with Sununu’s $6m.

Republican outside groups have also outspent Democrats, $37m to $20m, as both parties compete for the open seat.

Recent polls have consistently shown Pappas leading Sununu by five to eight percentage points.

articles.title: Anna Eskamani is bringing the ‘Mamdani Model’ to Central Florida
articles.summary: If Eskamani wins her mayoral bid next year, progressive Democrats will have another municipal toehold in the largely red Sunbelt.
articles.body:
As the hours tick down to the Nov. 3 midterm elections, Anna Eskamani continues her methodical, grassroots campaign for Orlando mayor in next year’s election .

If Eskamani wins, progressive Democrats will have another municipal toehold in the largely red Sunbelt.

Numerous U.S. mayors and would-be mayors aspire to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s mantle, marketing themselves as “another Mamdani” or “the next Mamdani.” Term-limited after eight years in the Florida House of Representatives, Eskamani, 36, also hopes to replicate Mamdani’s victorious 2025 campaign, applying his organizational playbook.

For Eskamani, a progressive Democrat and child of immigrants, a victory in the diverse 340,000-people resort city would culminate a nearly decade-long march.

“Power matters only if you use it to make life better for people and close the gap between what people earn and what it costs to live here,” she said after Orlando magazine recently named her the third most powerful person in the city. “That’s the work I’ve done in Tallahassee, and it’s the work I’ll bring to City Hall.”

She is hardworking, upbeat and relentlessly optimistic, which energizes volunteers and supporters. By January 2026, her campaign had knocked on more than 33,000 Orlando doors and raised a $1.4 million war chest , mostly in small $50 and $100 donations.

“I’m definitely an optimist and believe there is good in people and that people can change, that you can persuade people,” she told me in a telephone interview.

Volunteer Elly Kennedy, 50, now a realtor, met Eskamani in the mid-2010s when both worked at Planned Parenthood. “She was a real hard-working woman in a field that wasn’t the easiest,” Kennedy said. “She always had smile on her face.”

“I am a fan of her philosophy that we build from the ground up. It’s really a good feeling to have hope,” said Kennedy.

Longtime Orlando Democratic political consultant and former Florida legislator Dick Batchelor was impressed when first encountering Eskamani in 2018: “Even then she had firm grasp of the legislative issues. She had basically prepared herself for the legislative race, unlike other first-time candidates.”

Eskamani is both team player and insurgent. Even though she is not on this cycle’s ballot, she mobilized her network to canvas for Democratic turnout Nov. 3, and hosted a University of Central Florida candidate forum featuring Angie Nixon, a Senate hopeful who is affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America, as well as more moderate statewide candidates.

“She is very generous with her political capital,” said Batchelor.

University of Central Florida political scientist Aubrey Jewett taught the undergraduate Eskamani and served on her doctoral dissertation committee. “She is the kind of person that you want to help,” he recalled. “My first impression was that she was especially bright and energetic … [with] tremendous people skills.”

As a mayoral candidate, he said “she has, as the young people say, the ‘rizz’ — charisma. She’s good at explaining things in a non-technical way. She has a magnetic personality and a compelling personal story. … She is very positive and optimistic and hopeful.”

Eskamani was one of 48 first-time women candidates pictured on a 2018 Time magazine cover. The New York Times featured her as well. She was also featured in a prescient profile in The Atlantic by David Graham, complete with her smiling photo , headlined, “Hundreds of progressive, state-level candidates running in 2018 could pull the Democratic Party leftward for years to come.”

“If Eskamani beats her Republican opponent in November,” Graham wrote in 2018, “she’ll join a class of progressive candidates whose elections will reshape the Democratic Party. … Once in office, they will pull the Democratic Party leftward for years to come.”

And so she has, winning her initial legislative race — endorsed by Barack Obama, Orlando Mayor Buddy Dyer and the state AFL-CIO — and then reelected three times by healthy margins, until term-limited this year.

Mamdani and Eskamani do have differences, however.

Eskamani eschews ideological labels and is not a Democratic Socialists of America member. She supports a two-state Israel/Palestine solution but characterizes the Israeli war in Gaza as genocide. She recognizes the latter position creates “a difficulty for my Jewish brothers and sisters.”

Unlike Mamdani, Eskamani has had few campaign trail questions on the divisive issue, which has bedeviled numerous other Mamdani wannabes.

Growing up in working-class circumstances deeply affected Eskamani’s progressive politics. Her immigrant parents fled Iran separately as teenagers, Baha’i faith members, and met in Orlando. Their mother’s cancer death when she was 13 deeply impacted Anna.

“I had a very challenging but loving childhood,” she recalls. “I grew up watching my parents work multiple jobs just to keep up, and too many families here are living that same story right now.”

“Deep within me [lies] a source of focus and energy and determination” that comes from her parents, especially her mother, Eskamani said. “That was the unshakable core for me, the level of love she had for me.”

Her father supported his University of Central Florida electrical engineering studies by table waiting and often left the country working for long periods during their youth. Later he worked weekends as a Disney customer rep.

In each campaign, she focuses on economics, jobs, health care, homelessness. She also champions the local gay and transgender community. Conventional wisdom is that her relentless campaigning has so far preempted the field for the 2027 mayoral election.

How would Eskamani compare herself to Mamdani?

“We are both happy warriors, both committed to our communities in New York and Orlando. We believe in mass public engagement as the most effective way to govern, and we believe that poverty is a policy issue.”

Mark I. Pinsky is a journalist and author based in Durham, N.C.

articles.title: El-Sayed accuses Stevens of ‘relitigating’ primary after calls for apology on Israel
articles.summary: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) is firing back on his former primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), after she expected him to apologize over his comments on Israel just a few days out from the high-stakes Michigan Senate race. Stevens said would appear alongside El-Sayed for the first time since their August primary this…
articles.body:
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) is firing back on his former primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), after she expected him to apologize over his comments on Israel just a few days out from the high-stakes Michigan Senate race.

Stevens said would appear alongside El-Sayed for the first time since their August primary this weekend but criticized him over his response to a controversial anti-Israel ad that appeared to link the country to high U.S. grocery prices.

“So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand: that’s beating Mike Rogers, holding Trump accountable, and getting money out of politics,” El-Sayed said in a statement posted to the social platform X.

Support for Israel was a focal point of the widely watched Senate primary, with Stevens backed by millions from pro-Israel lobbying groups.

Since the primary, Stevens has supported El-Sayed and endorsed him immediately after. But Stevens’s fiancé, who is Jewish, recently said he would vote for former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers over El-Sayed.

Stevens reaffirmed that she would support El-Sayed in a CNN interview on Wednesday but said some Michigan voters are “hurt” and “confused” about the ad linking Israel to grocery prices.

She said in a statement on Friday that El-Sayed did not denounce the ad forcefully enough and expected him to apologize.

“The ad did not invent its argument; it dramatized one Dr. El-Sayed has made in his own words throughout this campaign: that Israel is the reason Michigan cannot afford schools, healthcare, and child care,” Stevens said. “I therefore expect him to apologize for those statements as well.”

Rogers has courted disaffected Democrats, mainly Jewish voters, as part of his effort to win Michigan in a Democratic-leaning year.

Stevens said she accepted an invitation from Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.), a major leader in the Black and Christian communities, to appear alongside the congressman and El-Sayed in a Detroit church service on Sunday.

The Hill reached out to both Stevens and El-Sayed to see if the joint appearance will continue as planned.
